case_studies.title: Stop Shipping AI Agents on Faith: Capability Is Not Production Readiness
case_studies.abstract: AI agents are moving into production workflows where they retrieve information, call tools, maintain state, and act on behalf of users or organizations, but many release decisions still rely on capability signals, demos, or behavioral tests that do not show whether an agent is ready to operate under production constraints. Capability is therefore not production readiness. This paper introduces the ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness index for AI agents. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of determining if AI agents are ready for production use, the authors built the ProofAgent Index (PAI) to assess governance readiness, and the result is a framework to evaluate AI agents' production readiness. The PAI combines four dimensions of deployment evidence to ensure AI agents can operate under production constraints. This research aims to improve the reliability of AI agents in production workflows.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI agent deployments, here is what to do: assess your current evaluation process, review the PAI framework, and apply its four dimensions to ensure your AI agents are production ready. This flags a risk: if your organization uses AI agents in production, check their production readiness immediately using the PAI framework. The PAI framework is directly applicable to IT infrastructure work involving AI agent deployments.
case_studies.relevance_tag: AI governance, production readiness, agent deployment
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty in the novel concept of PAI, relevant to IT engineers, and actionable in 90 days. Novelty in IT relevance and potential for real-world impact on agent deployment decisions.

case_studies.title: Cybersecurity Detection Classification with Reasoning-enabled Language Models
case_studies.abstract: A major issue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) is alert fatigue, as the number of detections reported is more than staff can triage in a given day. Prior work prompts or fine-tunes large language models (LLMs) to emit a triage label directly, but does not train them to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat. We train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections by combining automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. We find that CoT reasoning also degrade
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of alert fatigue in Security Operations Centers by building a reasoning-enabled language model that can triage detections and identify genuine threats, resulting in improved accuracy. The model was trained on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections using a combination of automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning. This can help reduce the number of false positives and improve cybersecurity detection classification.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage a Security Operations Center, here is what to do: review your current triage process, consider implementing a reasoning-enabled language model to improve detection classification, and assess the potential for reducing alert fatigue and improving threat identification. This flags a risk: if your org uses manual triage processes, check your detection classification accuracy immediately. If you don't manage a Security Operations Center, this research is not directly applicable to your IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper scores highly for IT Relevance (20) since it directly deals with security in a SaaS/endpoint management context. It does show some Novelty as it introduces CoT reasoning to LLMs. Value in 90 days is high because the results can be applied to existing SOC infrastructures.

case_studies.title: RoboBRIDGE: A Modular Framework for Bridging Policies to Robust Real-World Robotic Agents
case_studies.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have attracted growing interest as a scalable approach to robotic manipulation. While these models are effective action predictors, deploying them as robotic agents exposes critical gaps: no mechanism for failure recovery, inconsistent execution over long horizons, and limited robustness to shifts in observations, tasks, or embodiments. Existing solutions address these limitations individually through model retraining or environment-specific modules, yet what is needed is a general framework that systematically transforms a pretrained VLA into a robotic agen
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of robotic agents' lack of robustness and reliability in real-world scenarios by building a modular framework called RoboBRIDGE. The framework transforms pretrained Vision-Language-Action models into robust robotic agents. The result is a more reliable and consistent robotic agent that can recover from failures and adapt to changes.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on robotic agents and Vision-Language-Action models, which are not typically used in cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: PAPER EXTRACTS: Novelty score 20 - IT engineers would forward due to its application in robotics. IT Relevance score 10 - directly affects robotic agent work, but limited to robotics, not widely deployed in IT infrastructure.

case_studies.title: Beyond Sentiment: Structured Information Extraction from Financial News
case_studies.abstract: Financial sentiment analysis has become a standard component in news-driven stock prediction, yet it reduces rich, multi-dimensional news articles to a single polarity score. We hypothesize that financial news encodes multiple orthogonal information dimensions---event type, impact scope, temporal horizon, and semantic confidence---that sentiment alone cannot capture, and that these dimensions carry independent predictive value. To test this hypothesis, we propose a structured information extraction framework that leverages LLaMA-3.1-70B to extract six semantic dimensions from financial news. T
case_studies.summary: This research extracts structured information from financial news to improve stock predictions, going beyond simple sentiment analysis by identifying multiple dimensions such as event type and impact scope. The team built a framework using LLaMA-3.1-70B to extract six semantic dimensions from financial news. The result is a more nuanced understanding of financial news that can inform investment decisions.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, but can inform data analytics or business intelligence projects that rely on financial news data, which may be of interest to IT teams supporting these areas.

case_studies.title: AgentRadio: Passive Awareness for Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Collaboration
case_studies.abstract: Understanding large codebases is a long-horizon task for Large Language Model (LLM) agents: answering a single question can require building and running the software, tracing execution across files, and synthesizing evidence over tens of minutes. On SWE-Atlas QnA, a benchmark of long-horizon questions over production repositories, a single Claude Code agent (Opus 4.6) resolves only 32.3% of tasks. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of understanding large codebases by multiple agents working together, building a system called AgentRadio that enables passive awareness for long-horizon multi-agent collaboration, resulting in improved task resolution rates. The system allows agents to share knowledge and adapt to each other's findings. This is relevant to IT work in managing complex software development projects.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage large-scale software development projects, here is what to do: consider implementing a collaborative system like AgentRadio to improve code comprehension and task resolution rates among your development teams, assess your current codebase management tools for potential integration with such a system, and evaluate the potential benefits of agent-based collaboration for your specific use case.
case_studies.score_reasoning: AgentRadio explores a problem relevant to IT engineers (LLM agents in long-horizon tasks), but its specific scope (code comprehension on benchmarks) is relatively narrow. However, the authors hint at a possible solution (dividing work among agents) that could be leveraged by IT engineers in the future.

case_studies.title: Would You Walk to the Car Wash? Revealing the Salience Bias of Large Language Models in Commonsense Reasoning
case_studies.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance in complex reasoning tasks, they have learned to heavily prioritize explicit conditions provided in the input. However, in everyday commonsense reasoning, this mechanism exposes a critical vulnerability which we term Salience Bias: models become easily hijacked by useless explicit distractors (e.g., numerical values), leading them to ignore the implicit physical or commonsense prerequisites of a task. A critical open question is whether this failure reflects a genuine gap in commonsense knowledge or merely its suppression under misleading tas
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models being misled by irrelevant information, the authors built a test to reveal this Salience Bias, and the result shows models can be hijacked by useless explicit distractors. It does not directly relate to managing cloud infrastructure. The research focuses on the limitations of language models in everyday reasoning tasks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: Reveals a surprising behavior of LLMs. IT Relevance: Discusses a potential weakness relevant to LLMs deployment. Value within 90 days: This might affect how IT engineers evaluate and work with LLMs.

case_studies.title: Agents That Certify Their Own Exploits: Confidence-Scheduled Restricted Responses for Safe Opponent Exploitation
case_studies.abstract: An agent playing a Nash-equilibrium strategy in a two-player zero-sum imperfect-information game secures the game value but forfeits the additional value offered by a flawed opponent. Diffuse deviations pose a particular challenge: binary release rules may gather too little evidence to act, while a full best response to an incomplete opponent model can be highly exploitable. We introduce \emph{budget-constrained confidence-scheduled restricted responses} (CS-RNR), the first opponent-exploitation method whose safety guarantee is a certificate the agent computes on the strategy it actually deplo
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of safely exploiting an opponent's weaknesses in competitive games without forfeiting the game value, by introducing a new method called budget-constrained confidence-scheduled restricted responses. The researchers built a system that allows an agent to compute a safety guarantee certificate for its own strategy. The result is a more effective and safe way to play against flawed opponents.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on game theory and artificial intelligence in competitive games, rather than cloud infrastructure management or IT consulting.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty score: paper introduces a new concept but it's not directly related to IT infrastructure or deployment. However, the use of Nash-equilibrium and zero-sum imperfect-information games might have some indirect implications. Relevance score: 18. Value_90_days: 15. Paper does not offer clear actionables for IT engineers but might be of interest to researchers with potential long-term implications for AI deployment.

case_studies.title: PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks
case_studies.abstract: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used for evaluating LLM's issue resolution capability. They typically follow a common construction pipeline: each PR (Pull Request) is paired with its linked issue by extracting issue references from the PR description; the issue description is used as the problem statement, and the PR patch serves as the test oracle. However, due to the inherent complexity of developing and maintaining large repositories, such PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned in practice. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of misaligned pull requests and issues in software development, building a tool called PAIChecker to identify and check these misalignments, resulting in a finding that 13.6% of instances exhibit misalignment. The tool helps improve the accuracy of software development benchmarks. This research is primarily focused on software development and testing.

case_studies.score_reasoning: This paper deals with potential misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks for LLMs, which are relevant to IT as they impact the evaluation of Large Language Models, especially those used in DevOps or SWE. However, the paper itself may not necessarily contribute to the construction of a new IT service or automation of a task within 90 days. case_studies.title: Correcting Mode Collapse in Silicon Sampling with Semantic Similarity Rating
case_studies.abstract: Silicon sampling refers to the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate responses to surveys. It has shown promise, but tends to generate response distributions with unrealistically low variance. We argue that this mode collapse is due to LLMs failure to generate numeric data, and that text responses may be better suited for this task. We analyze whether Semantic Similarity Rating can improve the fidelity of silicon sampling responses when asked about political attitudes. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of mode collapse in silicon sampling by using Semantic Similarity Rating to improve response fidelity. The authors built a method that uses text embeddings to map text responses from Large Language Models to a numeric scale. The result shows promise in generating more realistic response distributions.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it relates to improving survey response generation using Large Language Models.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty is moderate because it deals with LLMs and mode collapse. IT relevance is medium because it touches on LLMs, but the deployment angle is weak. Value 90 days is low because the solution is specific to survey responses and lacks wider applicability.

case_studies.title: ViewMind3D: Modular View-Aware Inference for Training-Free 3D-QA
case_studies.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled new possibilities for 3D question answering (3D-QA), a key capability for embodied AI and robotic perception. However, most existing methods rely on 3D-specific training or fine-tuning with costly annotations, limiting their scalability and real-world applicability. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of 3D question answering without requiring costly 3D-specific training or annotations. The authors built ViewMind3D, a modular framework for 3D spatial reasoning over multi-view observations of a scene. The result is a fully training-free framework for 3D-QA tasks.

case_studies.title: ORCA-bench: How Ready Are Language Model Agents for Oncall?
case_studies.abstract: Large language models can write, patch, and search code, but oncall root cause analysis (RCA) demands something different: reasoning over noisy metrics, logs, traces, and source code, starting from ambiguous user-facing reports, often hours after the incident began. We introduce ORCA-bench, a benchmark that puts general-purpose coding agents in a production-fidelity oncall setting. ORCA-bench pairs a live OpenTelemetry-instrumented microservice system--exposing six days of metrics, logs, and traces through real telemetry interfaces (Prometheus, Jaeger, and OpenSearch via Grafana) and full sour
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of using large language models for oncall root cause analysis, by building a benchmark called ORCA-bench to test their ability to reason over noisy metrics and logs. The result is a production-fidelity oncall setting that pairs a live microservice system with real telemetry interfaces. This helps assess the readiness of language model agents for oncall duties.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage oncall systems or use large language models for incident analysis, here is what to do: review the ORCA-bench benchmark to understand its capabilities, assess your current oncall tools and processes, and consider integrating ORCA-bench to improve root cause analysis. This flags a risk: if your org relies on language models for oncall, check their performance using ORCA-bench immediately. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work outside of oncall and incident analysis.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLM agents in an oncall setting, which is relevant to IT operations. However, its novelty is limited, and its value in the next 90 days is indirect.

case_studies.title: CoGate: Confidence-Gated Co-Decoding for Secure Code Generation
case_studies.abstract: Large language models are widely used for code generation, but they can also produce insecure programs due to patterns learned from their pretraining data. Decoding-time steering has become an important solution to this problem: a small expert model is combined with the target model at each step to generate more secure code, which is referred to as co-decoding. However, the acceptance rule for existing co-decoding approaches does not consider the expert model's confidence. When the security expert is unconfident due to unseen patterns or out-of-distribution (OOD) contexts, its guidance can the
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models generating insecure code by building a confidence-gated co-decoding system called CoGate, which results in more secure code generation. CoGate combines a small expert model with the target model to generate code, taking into account the expert model's confidence. This research aims to improve the security of code generation using large language models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses large language models for code generation, here is what to do: review your current code generation process to identify potential security risks, consider implementing a co-decoding approach like CoGate, and evaluate the confidence of your expert model to ensure secure code generation. This flags a risk: if your org uses large language models for code generation, check the security of the generated code immediately. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to cloud infrastructure that uses code generation.
